shared_context.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be a continuously differentiable function defined for all real $x.$ Values for $f$ and some of its derivatives at particular points are shown below.

$$

$$

| **$x$** | **$f(x)$** | **${f}^{′}(x)$** | **${f}^{″}(x)$** | **${f}^{‴}(x)$** | **${f}^{(4)}(x)$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $9$ | $-1$ | $-5$ | $-4$ | $-2$ |
| $3$ | $6$ | $-5$ | $-6$ | $-6$ | $-3$ |
| $4$ | $-5$ | $-7$ | $∗$ | $-13$ | $-6$ |

$$

$$

In the interval $x\in [2,4],$ the function $f$ and its derivatives are all decreasing.

feedback.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We have $f(4)=-5$ and ${f}^{′}(4)=-7,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-5-7(x-4) \\  & =-5-7x+28 \\  & =-7x+23.\end{aligned}
$$

Our tangent line approximation is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-7x+23.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(4.1)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=4.1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4.1) & ≈L(4.1) \\  & =-7(4.1)+23 \\  & =-5.7.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=3,$ we plug $a=3$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(3)+{f}^{′}(3)(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(3)(x-3)^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $f(3)=6,$ ${f}^{′}(3)=-5,$ and ${f}^{″}(3)=-6$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =6-5(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(-6)(x-3)^{2} \\  & =6-5(x-3)-3(x-3)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our second-degree Taylor polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =6-5(x-3)-3(x-3)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(3.2)$ by evaluating the second-degree Taylor polynomial approximation at $x=3.2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.2) & ≈{P}_{2}(3.2) \\  & =6-5(3.2-3)-3(3.2-3)^{2} \\  & =6-5(0.2)-3(0.2)^{2} \\  & =4.88.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=4$ is given by

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(4)(x-4)^{2}.
$$

We're given an expansion about the point $x=4,$ so the coefficient of the second-degree term is $\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(4).$ In the given equation, we see that the coefficient of the second-degree term is $-5,$ so we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(4)=-5\,⟹\,{f}^{″}(4)=-10.
$$

The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4)+\frac{{f}^{″}(4)}{2!}(x-4)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(4)}{3!}(x-4)^{3} \\  & =f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4)+\frac{{f}^{″}(4)}{2}(x-4)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(4)}{6}(x-4)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We have the following set of values:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4)=-5 \\ {f}^{′}(4)=-7 \\ {f}^{″}(4)=-10 \\ {f}^{‴}(4)=-13\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given values into our Taylor Polynomial, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =-5-7(x-4)+\frac{(-10)}{2}(x-4)^{2}+\frac{(-13)}{6}(x-4)^{3} \\  & =-5-7(x-4)-5(x-4)^{2}-\frac{13}{6}(x-4)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The third-degree Taylor polynomial approximation is

$$
{P}_{3}(x)=-5-7(x-4)-5(x-4)^{2}-\frac{13}{6}(x-4)^{3}.
$$

We can approximate $f(3.9)$ by evaluating the third-degree Taylor polynomial approximation at $x=3.9.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.9) & ≈{P}_{3}(3.9) \\  & =-5-7(3.9-4)-5(3.9-4)^{2}-\frac{13}{6}(3.9-4)^{3} \\  & =-5-7(-0.1)-5(-0.1)^{2}-\frac{13}{6}(-0.1)^{3} \\  & ≈-4.348.\end{aligned}
$$
